narrative: A 29-year-old woman set out from Istanbul, where staying was no longer possible because even with a university degree finding a decent job was a fantasy. Her first stop was Izmir on the Aegean, where she stayed with Syrian neighbors while waiting for the smuggler. The first call to leave was canceled because the weather changed; the second day she packed and went, carrying a life jacket she had paid dearly for. The smuggler was angry that her bag was heavy and said she could not take it; she argued that a woman needs many things, unlike men. She paid 1,200 euros for the sea crossing to Greece. The trip was canceled again and she lost a 200-lira taxi fare. Two days later she found another smuggler. From a small mosque they were taken to an abandoned house, then packed into a big truck like a flock of sheep, and arrived at 9 p.m. at an empty stretch of shore where only wind and water could be heard. They were forbidden to talk or use flashlights, and put on their life jackets in the dark. The men inflated the boat by hand for about two hours, then they crept to the beach in silence. She thinks there were about 60 of them, counting the children. The men sat on the edges and the women at the bottom; she sat by the engine, nearest the water. They believed the trip would take an hour or two, but by GPS she realized they were still in a long narrow channel, not the sea; the engine snagged on weeds again and again. When they reached open water the Turkish driver was replaced by an Algerian refugee, who spun the boat in circles and made everyone panic until he got control. In the high waves, people's prayers rose as the boat climbed and fell; she thought it ironic that most people only remember God when in trouble. After two more hours they saw the lights of a Greek Coast Guard ship, which stayed behind them and lit the way to the island. After five dangerous hours they landed safe. She now lives in Minden, Germany, and was awaiting approval of a three-year residence visa.
